questions.question: Which HTTP status code should a server send when a client has crossed its rate limit?
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests is the standard code for a rate limit, often with a Retry-After header.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of a token bucket over a fixed window?
options: It needs no memory at all
It removes the burst at the edge of two windows
It works without a client key
questions.explanation: A token bucket refills steadily, so a client cannot send a double burst at a window edge.

questions.question: The limit is 3 requests per minute per client. One client sends 5 requests within 10 seconds. Which statuses do they get, in order?
questions.explanation: The first three fit in the limit. Requests four and five are over it and get 429.

questions.question: A token bucket has capacity 3 and refills 1 token per second. It is empty at time 0. How many calls pass at time 2 seconds?
questions.explanation: Two seconds add two tokens, so exactly two calls succeed and the third is rejected.

questions.question: An app with three running instances behind a load balancer uses an in-memory limiter of 100 calls per minute. Clients seem to make about 300. What is the problem?
options: Each instance counts separately, so the limit needs a shared store
The window should be one second
The limiter must use the IP address only
questions.explanation: In-memory counters live inside one instance. A shared store such as Redis, or a gateway limit, is needed.
